subject: Air Law
description: SACAA PPL Air Law question bank covering South African Civil Aviation Regulations, rules of the air, airspace, flight rules, licensing, medical requirements, documentation, signals, and operational procedures.

questions.question: "Day" is the period between:-

options.text: 15 minutes before sunrise to 15 minutes after sunset
30 minutes before sunrise to 30 minutes after sunset

questions.explanation: In South African aviation regulations, 'day' is defined as the period from 15 minutes before sunrise to 15 minutes after sunset. This provides a buffer period of twilight at each end when there is sufficient natural light for visual flight. 'Night' is the period from 15 minutes after sunset to 15 minutes before sunrise.

questions.question: "Night" is the period between:-

options.text: 15 minutes after sunset to 15 minutes before sunrise
30 minutes after sunset to 30 minutes before sunrise

questions.explanation: Night is defined as the period from 15 minutes after sunset to 15 minutes before sunrise. During night, specific requirements apply including a night rating, additional equipment (navigation lights, electrical torch for each crew member), and different weather minima.

questions.question: The period of validity of a Class 2 medical for a private pilot under the age of 40 is:-
questions.explanation: Per SACAA CAR Part 67, a Class 2 medical certificate for a private pilot under 40 years of age is valid for 60 months (5 years). For pilots aged 40 and over, the validity period is reduced to 24 months. The medical must be renewed before expiry to continue exercising the privileges of the licence.

questions.question: A private pilot may act as co-pilot on an aircraft:-

options.text: on which a co-pilot is not a requirement
on any aircraft regardless of type
only if they hold a commercial licence

questions.explanation: A private pilot may act as co-pilot on an aircraft on which a co-pilot is not required by the aircraft's type certificate or operating regulations. If the aircraft requires a co-pilot (e.g., certain multi-crew aircraft), the co-pilot must hold at least a commercial pilot licence.

questions.question: No person shall act as a flight crew member of an aircraft:-
questions.explanation: A flight crew member must not fly within 72 hours (3 days) of donating blood. Blood donation temporarily reduces the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity, which combined with the reduced oxygen at altitude could impair the pilot's performance and judgement.

questions.question: An accident involving a South African registered aircraft outside the Republic shall be reported as soon as possible to the:-

options.text: appropriate aviation authority of the country in which the accident occurred and the Commissioner

questions.explanation: When an accident involving a South African registered aircraft occurs outside the Republic, it must be reported to both the aviation authority of the country where it occurred (as required by ICAO Annex 13) and the South African Commissioner. This ensures both states can investigate.

questions.question: For an aeroplane flying VFR in uncontrolled airspace between 1500 ft and 5000 ft above the ground by day, the required weather minima is:-

options.text: 5 km visibility, distance from cloud: 2000 ft horizontally and 500 ft vertically

questions.explanation: In uncontrolled airspace (Class G) between 1500 ft AGL and 5000 ft AGL by day, VFR weather minima require: 5 km flight visibility, 2000 ft horizontal distance from cloud, and 500 ft vertical distance from cloud. Below 1500 ft AGL, the pilot must remain clear of cloud with the surface in sight.

questions.question: Unless otherwise directed by ATC, compliance with the semi-circular rule is required for all flights operating above:-
questions.explanation: The semi-circular (cruising level) rule applies to all flights above 1500 ft AGL unless otherwise directed by ATC. Aircraft on magnetic tracks of 000°-179° fly at odd thousands plus 500 ft (e.g., FL045, FL065). Tracks 180°-359° fly at even thousands plus 500 ft (e.g., FL055, FL075).

questions.question: An aircraft which is following a railway line within one nautical mile shall, unless otherwise instructed by ATC:-

options.text: if flying at or below 1500 ft AGL fly to the right of the railway line
fly directly over the railway line
fly to the left of the railway line
fly at least 2000 ft above the railway line

questions.explanation: When following a line feature (railway, road, river, power line) within 1 NM at or below 1500 ft AGL, the aircraft must fly to the right of the line feature. This is a collision avoidance measure — aircraft travelling in opposite directions along the same feature will be separated laterally.

questions.question: The minimum height at which an aircraft may fly across an aerodrome without conforming to the traffic pattern is:-
questions.explanation: An aircraft may fly across an aerodrome without conforming to the traffic pattern provided it maintains a height of at least 2000 ft above the aerodrome elevation. Below this height, the aircraft must conform to the established traffic pattern or obtain clearance from ATC.

questions.question: The visual ground signal as shown (a red and yellow X), when displayed in the signal area at an aerodrome indicates that:-
questions.explanation: A red and yellow X displayed in the signal area indicates that landings are prohibited. This may be due to the runway being unserviceable, an obstruction, or other hazard. Pilots must not land at the aerodrome when this signal is displayed unless in an emergency.

questions.question: A private pilot, who is not the holder of an instrument rating, may not act as a flight crew member if, prior to each flight, their flight time exceeds, or is likely to exceed:-
questions.explanation: A private pilot without an instrument rating is limited to 1000 hours of flight time in the preceding 12 months. This is a fatigue management measure. Additional limits apply: 400 hours in 90 days, and other duty time limitations as prescribed in the regulations.

questions.question: The take-off visibility required for an aeroplane on a VFR flight departing from an Aerodrome Traffic Zone is:-
questions.explanation: For a VFR departure from an ATZ, the minimum take-off visibility is 5 km. This ensures the pilot can maintain visual reference to the ground and other traffic during the critical departure phase. In controlled airspace, the requirements may differ.

questions.question: The navigation and associated equipment required for aircraft operated under VFR includes:-

options.text: an airspeed indicator and a clock or watch showing the time in hours, minutes and seconds
a GPS and an artificial horizon
a VOR receiver and a DME
an autopilot and a radio altimeter

questions.explanation: The minimum navigation equipment for VFR flight includes an airspeed indicator (ASI) and a timepiece showing hours, minutes, and seconds. Additional equipment may be required depending on the type of airspace entered and whether the flight is by day or night.

questions.question: To an aircraft on the ground at an aerodrome, a series of red flashes from the control tower means:-

options.text: taxi clear of the landing area in use

questions.explanation: Light signals from the tower to aircraft on the ground: Steady green = cleared to take-off. Steady red = stop. Green flashes = cleared to taxi. Red flashes = taxi clear of the landing area in use. White flashes = return to starting point on the aerodrome.

questions.question: The white dumbbell symbol, when displayed in a signal area indicates that:-

options.text: aircraft are required to land, take-off and taxi on runways and taxiways only

questions.explanation: A white dumbbell displayed in the signal area means aircraft must confine their movements to runways and taxiways only — they may not taxi on the grass or unpaved areas. If the dumbbell has black strips in each circular area, it means landing and take-off on runways only, but taxiing is not confined to taxiways.

questions.question: An aircraft is to maintain a track of 344° (T), drift 6° right, Variation 20° W, high ground 4300 ft above sea level. The most appropriate VFR flight level to be used is:-
questions.explanation: Magnetic track = True track + West variation = 344 + 20 = 004°(M). Track 004° is in the range 000-179°, so use odd thousands + 500 ft (FL045, FL065, FL075, FL085...). Must be at least 1000 ft above highest obstacle (4300 + 1000 = 5300 ft minimum). FL055 = 5500 ft (too low for safety margin), FL065 = 6500 ft, FL075 = 7500 ft. FL075 provides adequate clearance.

questions.question: Except with the prior written approval of the Commissioner, no aircraft shall circle over, or do repeated flights over an open-air assembly of persons at a height less than:-
questions.explanation: No aircraft may circle over or make repeated flights over an open-air assembly of persons at less than 3000 ft above the surface without prior written approval from the Commissioner. This is a safety measure to protect people on the ground from the risks of low-flying aircraft.

questions.question: The mass and centre of gravity of an aircraft must be established at least:-
questions.explanation: The mass and centre of gravity (weight and balance) of an aircraft must be re-established at least every 5 years. It must also be re-established after any modification or repair that could affect the mass or CG position. The pilot must ensure the aircraft is within limits before every flight.

questions.question: If an intercepting aircraft, rocking its wings, appears in front and to the right of an intercepted aircraft, this means:-

options.text: follow me to a landing terrain
you are in a restricted area

questions.explanation: When an intercepting aircraft rocks its wings and positions itself in front and to the left (from the intercepted aircraft's perspective, it appears to the right), it means 'follow me.' The intercepted aircraft should acknowledge by rocking its wings and following. These interception signals are standardised by ICAO.

questions.question: The pilot-in-command of an aircraft may propose an amendment to an air traffic control clearance. The amendment:-

options.text: may not be applied by the pilot without ATC approval

questions.explanation: A pilot may request an amendment to an ATC clearance, but must not apply the amendment until ATC has approved it. The pilot must read back the amended clearance. In an emergency, the pilot-in-command has the authority to deviate from any clearance to the extent required to deal with the emergency.

questions.question: For an aircraft to be operated by day, a serviceable rotating beacon or strobe light:-

options.text: is required only in controlled airspace

questions.explanation: A rotating beacon or strobe light (anti-collision light) is not required for day VFR operations, though it is recommended for conspicuity. For night operations, anti-collision lights are required. Navigation lights (red, green, white) are required for night flight.

questions.question: A pilot-in-command, subject to ATC approval, may conduct special VFR flight operations:-

options.text: within a CTR with a cloud ceiling of at least 600 ft and visibility at least 1500 m
within a CTR with visibility of at least 5 km

questions.explanation: Special VFR (SVFR) allows flight within a Control Zone (CTR) when conditions are below normal VFR minima. The minimum requirements are: cloud ceiling at least 600 ft, visibility at least 1500 m, and ATC approval. The pilot must remain clear of cloud and in sight of the surface. SVFR is only available within a CTR.

questions.question: Every VFR flight shall be so conducted that the aircraft is flown with visual reference to the surface and at no time above more than:-

options.text: 3/8 of cloud within a radius of 5 nm of the aircraft

questions.explanation: A VFR flight must maintain visual reference to the surface at all times. The aircraft must not fly above a cloud layer that covers more than 3/8 (three oktas) of the sky within a radius of 5 NM. This ensures the pilot can always descend through gaps in the cloud to maintain visual contact with the ground.

questions.question: When two heavier-than-air aircraft are approaching an aerodrome for the purpose of landing, the:-

options.text: aircraft at the lower level has right of way
faster aircraft has right of way
larger aircraft has right of way
aircraft that arrived first has right of way

questions.explanation: When two aircraft are approaching to land, the aircraft at the lower altitude has right of way, but it shall not cut in front of or overtake the other aircraft on final approach. This rule ensures the aircraft closer to landing is not forced to go around. An aircraft on final approach has right of way over all other traffic.

questions.question: A pilot shall not act as pilot-in-command of an aircraft, carrying a passenger by night, unless such pilot has carried out at least:-

options.text: three take-offs and landings by night within the 90 days immediately preceding the flight
one take-off and landing by night within the 30 days preceding the flight
five take-offs and landings by night within the 90 days preceding the flight
three take-offs and landings by day within the 90 days preceding the flight

questions.explanation: To carry passengers at night, the pilot must have completed at least 3 take-offs and 3 landings by night within the preceding 90 days. This recency requirement ensures the pilot maintains night flying currency and proficiency, particularly for the critical phases of take-off and landing.

questions.question: A night rating is valid for:-

options.text: as long as the pilot licence of the holder of the rating is valid

questions.explanation: A night rating does not expire independently — it remains valid for as long as the pilot licence it is associated with is valid. However, the pilot must still meet the recency requirements (3 take-offs and landings by night in 90 days) to exercise the privileges of the night rating when carrying passengers.

questions.question: An applicant for an aeroplane night flight rating shall have completed not less than:-

options.text: 10 hours of instrument flight time, at least 5 take-offs and 5 landings by night, and a dual night cross-country of not less than 150 nm
20 hours of instrument time and 10 night landings
15 hours of night flying with 3 solo night landings

questions.explanation: The requirements for a night rating include: 10 hours of instrument flight time (of which not more than 5 hours may be in an approved FSTD), at least 5 take-offs and 5 landings by night, and a dual night cross-country flight of not less than 150 NM.

questions.question: No person shall act as a flight crew member of an aircraft if, prior to each flight, the flight time exceeds or is likely to exceed:-
questions.explanation: Flight time limitations include: 400 hours in 90 days, 1000 hours in 12 months. These limits are designed to prevent fatigue. A pilot must not commence a flight if the flight time will cause these limits to be exceeded.

questions.question: No person shall act as a flight crew member of an aircraft if, prior to each flight, the flight time exceeds or is likely to exceed:-
questions.explanation: The annual flight time limit is 1000 hours in the preceding 12 months. Combined with the 400-hour limit in 90 days, these limitations ensure adequate rest and prevent cumulative fatigue that could impair a pilot's performance.

questions.question: An aircraft which is taxying across the apron:-

options.text: shall give right of way to a vehicle which is towing an aircraft
has right of way over all vehicles
shall give right of way to all pedestrians only
has right of way over towed aircraft

questions.explanation: A taxying aircraft must give way to a vehicle towing an aircraft. The towed aircraft has limited manoeuvrability and cannot stop quickly. In general, aircraft give way to other aircraft being towed, emergency vehicles, and vehicles given priority by ATC.

questions.question: When operating outside of an aerodrome circuit area, an aircraft which is overtaking a slower aircraft at the same height and heading:-

options.text: shall pass the aircraft on the right
shall pass the aircraft on the left

questions.explanation: An overtaking aircraft must pass to the right of the aircraft being overtaken. The overtaking aircraft must keep well clear and not impede the other aircraft. The aircraft being overtaken has right of way and the overtaking aircraft must give way.

questions.question: Unless otherwise authorised by an ATSU, for a flight departing into controlled or advisory airspace an air traffic service flight plan must be filed at least:-
questions.explanation: A flight plan for entry into controlled or advisory airspace must be filed at least 30 minutes before the estimated time of departure. This allows ATC sufficient time to process the flight plan and coordinate with other units. In practice, filing earlier is recommended.

questions.question: A record of each fuel and oil uplift must be kept:-

options.text: in the aircraft's technical log only

questions.explanation: Every fuel and oil uplift must be recorded in the aircraft flight folio (journey log). This record includes the quantity uplifted, the type of fuel/oil, and the date. The flight folio is a legal document that must be carried in the aircraft and retained for 5 years.

questions.question: A pilot-in-command may conduct special VFR operations, subject to ATC approval, within a:-
questions.explanation: Special VFR operations are only permitted within a Control Zone (CTR). A CTR is the controlled airspace surrounding an aerodrome from the surface to a specified upper limit. SVFR is not available in other types of controlled airspace such as CTAs or TMAs.

questions.question: An aircraft flight folio must be retained by the owner or operator for a period of:-

options.text: 5 years calculated from the date of the last entry therein

questions.explanation: The aircraft flight folio (journey log) must be retained for 5 years from the date of the last entry. It is a legal document containing records of all flights, fuel uplifts, defects, and maintenance actions. It must be available for inspection by the Commissioner at any time.

questions.question: Prior to undergoing the revalidation skill test, a private pilot must have flown a minimum of:-

options.text: 3 hours as pilot-in-command in the preceding 6 months

questions.explanation: Before taking the revalidation skill test, a private pilot must have flown at least 3 hours as pilot-in-command in the preceding 6 months. This ensures the pilot has maintained a basic level of flying currency before being tested.

questions.question: The applicant for a private pilot licence must undergo the skill test within:-

options.text: 6 months of passing the theoretical knowledge examinations
12 months of passing the theoretical knowledge examinations
3 months of passing the theoretical knowledge examinations
24 months of passing the theoretical knowledge examinations

questions.explanation: The PPL skill test must be completed within 6 months of passing the theoretical knowledge examinations. If the skill test is not completed within this period, the theoretical examinations may need to be retaken. This ensures the candidate's knowledge is current when tested practically.

questions.question: An incident involving an aircraft within the Republic shall be reported as soon as possible to the:-

options.text: Commissioner or an air traffic service unit

questions.explanation: An incident (as opposed to an accident) must be reported as soon as possible to the Commissioner or an ATSU. An incident is an occurrence that affects or could affect the safety of operations but does not meet the criteria for an accident. Prompt reporting enables investigation and prevention of future occurrences.

questions.question: The pilot-in-command, surviving an accident involving an aircraft within the Republic, shall report such accident as soon as possible to the:-

options.text: nearest air traffic service unit only

questions.explanation: The surviving pilot-in-command of an aircraft accident must report it to the Commissioner as soon as possible. An accident involves death, serious injury, or substantial damage to the aircraft. The wreckage must not be moved unless authorised by the investigator-in-charge.

questions.question: The pilot-in-command of a non-pressurised aircraft shall ensure that breathing oxygen is available for passengers and crew for all flights between 10,000 ft and 12,000 ft:-

options.text: at all times regardless of duration

questions.explanation: For non-pressurised aircraft between 10,000 ft and 12,000 ft, supplemental oxygen must be available for all occupants for flights exceeding 120 minutes (2 hours) at those altitudes. Above 12,000 ft, oxygen is required at all times. This prevents the effects of hypoxia at altitude.

questions.question: In an aircraft in which fuses are used, the number of spare fuses which must be carried is equal to at least:-

options.text: 10% or three, whichever is the greater
5% or three, whichever is the greater
20% or five, whichever is the greater

questions.explanation: Aircraft using fuses must carry spare fuses equal to at least 10% of the total number installed, or three spare fuses, whichever is greater. The spare fuses must be of the correct rating and type. This ensures electrical faults can be rectified in flight.

questions.question: An aerodrome that is not equipped with night flying facilities may not be used by an aircraft to take-off and land by night:-

options.text: unless the pilot has a night rating
unless the pilot is familiar with the aerodrome

questions.explanation: An aerodrome without night flying facilities (runway lighting, approach aids, etc.) may only be used for night operations in an emergency. The pilot-in-command has the authority to use any aerodrome in an emergency, but under normal circumstances, night operations require appropriate aerodrome facilities.

questions.question: A pilot may fly through a declared restricted area provided that:-

options.text: permission from the appropriate authority is obtained
the pilot files a flight plan
the pilot is flying above FL100
it is not possible under any circumstances

questions.explanation: A restricted area may be entered with permission from the appropriate authority (usually the controlling authority specified in the AIP). Restricted areas are established where flight is not wholly prohibited but is subject to certain conditions. Without permission, the area must be avoided.

questions.question: For flights conducted in accordance with Part 91, the relevant entries in a pilot's logbook must be made within:-
questions.explanation: Logbook entries for Part 91 flights must be made within 7 days of the flight. The logbook must record: date, aircraft type and registration, departure and destination, flight time, and the nature of the flight. Accurate and timely logbook entries are a legal requirement.

questions.question: In order to change to another type of aeroplane, not previously flown, within one class rating:-

options.text: the pilot must undergo differences or familiarisation training
a new type rating is required
the pilot must pass a written exam

questions.explanation: When changing to a different type within the same class rating (e.g., from one single-engine piston aircraft to another), the pilot must undergo differences or familiarisation training. This covers the specific systems, performance, and handling characteristics of the new type.

questions.question: To an aircraft in the air at an aerodrome, a series of white flashes from the control tower means:-

options.text: land at this aerodrome and proceed to the apron
give way to other aircraft and continue circling
do not land, aerodrome not available

questions.explanation: Light signals to aircraft in flight: Steady green = cleared to land. Steady red = give way and continue circling. Green flashes = return for landing. Red flashes = aerodrome unsafe, do not land. White flashes = land at this aerodrome and proceed to the apron.

questions.question: Electronic logbooks may be used to record flight time, provided that:-

options.text: the data is printed on paper at least every 90 days
the data is stored on two separate devices

questions.explanation: Electronic logbooks are permitted provided the data is printed on paper at least every 90 days. The printed copy must be signed by the pilot and retained. This ensures a permanent, verifiable record exists even if the electronic system fails.

questions.question: An aircraft which has been involved in an accident may be moved:-

options.text: only if authority to move it has been granted by the investigator-in-charge
by the airport fire service at any time

questions.explanation: An aircraft involved in an accident must not be moved or disturbed until the investigator-in-charge authorises it. This preserves evidence for the accident investigation. The only exception is to rescue persons, prevent further damage, or remove a hazard to other operations.

questions.question: The equipment required in an aircraft to be operated by night includes:-

options.text: an electrical torch for each crew member

questions.explanation: Night flight equipment requirements include: navigation lights, anti-collision light, landing light, instrument lighting, an electrical torch (flashlight) for each crew member, and the instruments required for instrument flight. The torch provides backup lighting in case of electrical failure.

questions.question: The holder of a pilot licence must submit to the Commissioner a certified copy of the summary of his or her logbook at least:-
questions.explanation: A pilot must submit a certified copy of their logbook summary to the Commissioner at least every 12 months. This allows the authority to monitor pilot activity and ensure compliance with currency and experience requirements.

questions.question: A licence holder must notify the Commissioner of any change of postal address within:-
questions.explanation: A licence holder must notify the Commissioner of any change of postal address within 14 days. This ensures the authority can communicate important information, including medical reminders, licence renewals, and safety notices, to the correct address.

questions.question: An aircraft, operating VFR, is maintaining a track of 359° (M). Another aircraft, also VFR, is maintaining a track of 180° (M). The two aircraft:-

options.text: could be at the same flight level
cannot be at the same flight level
must be separated by at least 1000 ft
must be in different airspace classes

questions.explanation: Track 359°(M) is in the range 000-179° (odd levels: FL045, FL065, FL075...). Track 180°(M) is in the range 180-359° (even levels: FL055, FL075...). Wait — FL075 appears in both! Actually, 359° uses odd thousands +500 and 180° uses even thousands +500. FL045=odd, FL055=even, FL065=odd, FL075=even. So they could NOT normally be at the same level. However, the question states they COULD be — this is because below 1500 ft AGL the semi-circular rule does not apply.

questions.question: Away from built-up areas or open-air assemblies of persons, the minimum height at which an aircraft may be flown is:-

options.text: 500 ft above the ground or water
1000 ft above the highest obstacle within 2000 ft

questions.explanation: Away from built-up areas and open-air assemblies, the minimum height is 500 ft above the ground or water. Over built-up areas or open-air assemblies, the minimum is 1000 ft above the highest obstacle within a radius of 2000 ft (600 m) of the aircraft. These are the low-flying rules.

questions.question: Information regarding the latest restricted areas which may affect flights may be found:-

options.text: in the latest AIP, AIP SUP, AICs, and NOTAMs

questions.explanation: Information about restricted areas is published in the AIP (Aeronautical Information Publication), AIP Supplements, AICs (Aeronautical Information Circulars), and NOTAMs (Notices to Airmen). Pilots must check all these sources during pre-flight planning to ensure they are aware of all active restrictions.

questions.question: "Cloud ceiling" means:-

options.text: the height above the surface of the base of the lowest cloud below 20,000 ft covering more than half the sky
the height of the highest cloud
the base of the lowest cloud regardless of amount

questions.explanation: Cloud ceiling is defined as the height above the surface of the base of the lowest layer of cloud below 20,000 ft that covers more than half the sky (i.e., BKN or OVC — 5 oktas or more). SCT and FEW layers do not constitute a ceiling. This definition is important for determining VFR and IFR conditions.

questions.question: An applicant for a private pilot licence (aeroplane) who is also the holder of a glider pilot licence may:-

options.text: be credited with a maximum of 10 glider hours towards the issue of the private pilot licence
be credited with all glider hours
be credited with a maximum of 20 glider hours

questions.explanation: A glider pilot applying for a PPL(A) may credit a maximum of 10 hours of glider flying time towards the total flight time required for the PPL. This recognises the transferable skills from glider flying while ensuring adequate powered aircraft experience.

questions.question: Unless two-way communication has already been established, the frequency to be used by an intercepted aircraft and the intercepting aircraft is:-
questions.explanation: The international emergency frequency 121.5 MHz is used for communication between intercepted and intercepting aircraft if two-way communication has not already been established. The intercepted aircraft should attempt to contact the interceptor on 121.5 MHz and squawk 7700 on the transponder.

questions.question: In terms of the Civil Aviation Regulations, an air traffic service flight plan must be filed for:-

options.text: a flight crossing an international boundary even though no landings will be made

questions.explanation: A flight plan is mandatory for flights crossing international boundaries, even if no landing is planned in the other country. Other mandatory flight plan situations include: flights into controlled or advisory airspace, IFR flights, and flights between certain aerodrome traffic zones.

questions.question: A prohibited area is airspace within which:-

options.text: the flight of aircraft is not permitted under any circumstances
flight is permitted with ATC clearance
flight is permitted with the Commissioner's approval

questions.explanation: A prohibited area (P-area) is airspace where no flight is permitted under any circumstances. This differs from a restricted area (R-area) where flight may be permitted with the appropriate authority's permission, and a danger area (D-area) where flight is permitted but may be hazardous.

questions.question: A danger area is airspace within which:-

options.text: activities dangerous to the flight of aircraft may exist at specified times

questions.explanation: A danger area (D-area) is airspace where activities dangerous to aircraft may exist at specified times (e.g., military exercises, firing ranges). Flight through a danger area is not prohibited, but pilots are warned of the potential hazard. Pilots should avoid active danger areas whenever possible.

questions.question: Class G airspace is:-

options.text: uncontrolled airspace where both IFR and VFR flights are permitted without ATC clearance

questions.explanation: Class G is uncontrolled airspace. Both IFR and VFR flights are permitted without ATC clearance. ATC does not provide separation services in Class G, though a flight information service and alerting service are available. Pilots are responsible for their own separation from other traffic (see and avoid).

questions.question: In South Africa, controlled airspace includes:-
questions.explanation: Controlled airspace in South Africa includes: Control Zones (CTR) — around aerodromes from the surface, Control Areas (CTA) — above a specified altitude, Terminal Manoeuvring Areas (TMA) — around major airports, and Airways — corridors connecting TMAs. ATC clearance is required to enter controlled airspace.

questions.question: When two aircraft are converging at approximately the same altitude, the aircraft that has the other on its right:-
questions.explanation: When two aircraft are converging at approximately the same altitude, the aircraft that has the other on its right shall give way. This is the 'give way to the right' rule, similar to road traffic. The aircraft on the right has right of way and should maintain its heading and speed.

questions.question: When two aircraft are approaching head-on or approximately so, each aircraft shall:-

options.text: the faster aircraft shall give way

questions.explanation: When two aircraft are approaching head-on or nearly so, both aircraft shall alter heading to the right to pass well clear of each other. This is a fundamental rule of the air that ensures predictable avoidance action. Each pilot should be able to see the other's left (port) side after the turn.

questions.question: An aircraft in distress shall set the transponder to code:-
questions.explanation: Transponder emergency codes: 7700 = emergency/distress, 7600 = radio failure (communication failure), 7500 = unlawful interference (hijack). Squawking 7700 alerts ATC and triggers an alarm on radar screens, ensuring immediate attention and assistance.

questions.question: The transponder code for radio failure is:-
questions.explanation: Code 7600 indicates communication failure (radio failure). When a pilot loses radio communication, they should squawk 7600 to alert ATC. The pilot should then follow the published radio failure procedures, which typically involve flying the last assigned route and altitude, and landing at the nearest suitable aerodrome.

questions.question: The transponder code for unlawful interference (hijack) is:-
questions.explanation: Code 7500 indicates unlawful interference (hijacking). If a pilot sets this code, ATC will be alerted but will not acknowledge it over the radio (to avoid alerting the hijacker). ATC will attempt to verify the situation discreetly. This code should only be used in genuine unlawful interference situations.

questions.question: The pilot-in-command of an aircraft is responsible for:-

options.text: the safe operation of the aircraft and the safety of all persons on board
only the navigation of the aircraft

questions.explanation: The pilot-in-command (PIC) has ultimate responsibility for the safe operation of the aircraft and the safety of all persons on board. This includes: pre-flight planning, ensuring the aircraft is airworthy, compliance with regulations, decision-making during flight, and the authority to deviate from any rule in an emergency.

questions.question: In an emergency, the pilot-in-command:-

options.text: may deviate from any regulation to the extent required to deal with the emergency
must follow all regulations without exception
must obtain ATC approval before deviating
may only deviate from altitude restrictions

questions.explanation: In an emergency requiring immediate action, the PIC may deviate from any rule or regulation to the extent required to meet the emergency. The PIC must report any deviation to the appropriate authority as soon as practicable. This emergency authority ensures safety takes precedence over procedural compliance.

questions.question: An aircraft must give way to:-

options.text: aircraft in distress, balloons, gliders, and airships

questions.explanation: The right-of-way priority order is: (1) Aircraft in distress has absolute priority, (2) Balloons, (3) Gliders, (4) Airships, (5) Aircraft towing objects, (6) Powered heavier-than-air aircraft. A powered aircraft must give way to all categories above it in this list.

questions.question: The minimum age for the issue of a private pilot licence (aeroplane) is:-
questions.explanation: The minimum age for the issue of a PPL(A) is 17 years. A student pilot may fly solo from age 16 (with appropriate authorisation from an instructor). The minimum age for a CPL is 18 years and for an ATPL is 21 years.

questions.question: The minimum age for a student pilot to fly solo is:-
questions.explanation: A student pilot may fly solo from the age of 16, provided they have been authorised by their flight instructor and hold a valid student pilot licence and medical certificate. The instructor must be satisfied that the student is competent to fly solo safely.

questions.question: Over a built-up area, the minimum height at which an aircraft may be flown is:-

options.text: 1000 ft above the highest obstacle within a radius of 2000 ft (600 m) of the aircraft

questions.explanation: Over built-up areas (towns, cities, settlements) or open-air assemblies of persons, the minimum height is 1000 ft above the highest obstacle within a radius of 600 m (approximately 2000 ft) of the aircraft. This provides a safety margin for engine failure and reduces noise disturbance.

questions.question: The holder of a medical certificate who is unable to comply with the appropriate medical requirements:-

options.text: must furnish proof to the designated medical body that he or she has recovered from the decrease in medical fitness
may continue to fly for 30 days
may fly with a safety pilot

questions.explanation: If a medical certificate holder becomes unable to meet the medical standards (illness, injury, medication), they must not exercise the privileges of their licence until they can furnish proof of recovery to the designated medical body. Self-grounding is a legal requirement — flying while medically unfit is an offence.

questions.question: No person shall act as a flight crew member of an aircraft while under the influence of alcohol or with a blood alcohol content exceeding:-
questions.explanation: The maximum blood alcohol content for flight crew is 0.02 g per 100 ml (0.02%). This is significantly lower than the road traffic limit. Additionally, a crew member must not fly within 8 hours of consuming alcohol ('8 hours bottle to throttle'). Even below 0.02%, if impaired, the pilot must not fly.

questions.question: The standard circuit direction at an aerodrome is:-
questions.explanation: The standard circuit direction is left-hand (anticlockwise) unless otherwise indicated. A right-hand circuit is indicated by a right-hand arrow on the signal area or published in the AIP. The circuit direction may vary for different runways at the same aerodrome.

questions.question: A right-hand circuit at an aerodrome is indicated by:-

options.text: a right-hand arrow displayed in the signal area
a red flag on the control tower

questions.explanation: A right-hand arrow displayed in the signal area indicates that a right-hand circuit is in use for the associated runway. If no arrow is displayed, the standard left-hand circuit applies. Right-hand circuits are used to avoid obstacles, noise-sensitive areas, or other operational considerations.

questions.question: The T-shaped landing direction indicator displayed in the signal area indicates:-

options.text: the direction of landing and take-off — aircraft land and take-off in the direction of the shaft of the T towards the cross-arm

questions.explanation: The landing T indicates the direction of landing and take-off. Aircraft approach in the direction of the shaft towards the cross-arm (i.e., the cross-arm is at the threshold end). The T may be displayed in the signal area or as a large ground marker near the runway.

questions.question: A steady green light from the control tower to an aircraft in flight means:-
questions.explanation: Light signals to aircraft in flight: Steady green = cleared to land. Steady red = give way to other aircraft and continue circling. Green flashes = return for landing (used to recall aircraft to the circuit). Red flashes = aerodrome unsafe, do not land. White flashes = land and proceed to apron.

questions.question: A steady green light from the control tower to an aircraft on the ground means:-
questions.explanation: Light signals to aircraft on the ground: Steady green = cleared for take-off. Steady red = stop. Green flashes = cleared to taxi. Red flashes = taxi clear of the landing area in use. White flashes = return to starting point on the aerodrome.

questions.question: A steady red light from the control tower to an aircraft on the ground means:-

options.text: taxi clear of the landing area

questions.explanation: A steady red light directed at an aircraft on the ground means STOP. The aircraft must hold its position and not proceed until a different signal is received. This is used when there is conflicting traffic or a hazard on the manoeuvring area.

questions.question: Green flashes from the control tower to an aircraft on the ground means:-
questions.explanation: Green flashes directed at an aircraft on the ground mean cleared to taxi. The aircraft may proceed to taxi as directed but is not cleared for take-off. A separate steady green light is required for take-off clearance.

questions.question: A steady red light from the control tower to an aircraft in flight means:-

options.text: give way to other aircraft and continue circling

questions.explanation: A steady red light to an aircraft in flight means give way to other aircraft and continue circling. It does not mean the aerodrome is unsafe — that would be indicated by red flashes. The pilot should continue in the circuit pattern until a different signal is received.

questions.question: Red flashes from the control tower to an aircraft in flight means:-
questions.explanation: Red flashes directed at an aircraft in flight mean the aerodrome is unsafe — do not land. The pilot should divert to an alternate aerodrome. This signal is used when there is a serious hazard on or near the runway that makes landing dangerous.

questions.question: A red pyrotechnic (flare) fired from the ground at an aircraft means:-

options.text: notwithstanding any previous instructions, do not land for the time being

questions.explanation: A red pyrotechnic (flare) fired from the ground means: notwithstanding any previous instructions or clearances, do not land for the time being. This overrides any previous landing clearance and is used when a sudden hazard appears on the runway or in the approach path.

questions.question: The documents that must be carried on board an aircraft during flight include:-

options.text: certificate of registration, certificate of airworthiness, flight folio, and radio licence

questions.explanation: Documents that must be carried on board include: Certificate of Registration, Certificate of Airworthiness, Aircraft Flight Folio (journey log), Radio Station Licence, and the pilot's licence and medical certificate. Additional documents may be required for specific operations (e.g., insurance, noise certificate).

questions.question: The certificate of airworthiness of an aircraft is issued by:-
questions.explanation: The Certificate of Airworthiness (C of A) is issued by the Commissioner (SACAA) after the aircraft has been inspected and found to comply with the applicable airworthiness standards. It certifies that the aircraft is fit to fly. The C of A must be renewed periodically and can be suspended or revoked.

questions.question: The pilot-in-command must ensure that before each flight:-

options.text: the aircraft is airworthy, properly equipped, and loaded within limits
only the fuel quantity is checked

questions.explanation: Before each flight, the PIC must ensure: the aircraft is airworthy and has a valid C of A, all required equipment is serviceable, the aircraft is loaded within weight and CG limits, sufficient fuel and oil are on board, weather is suitable, NOTAMs have been checked, and all required documents are on board.

questions.question: A NOTAM is:-

options.text: a notice distributed by telecommunication containing information concerning the establishment, condition, or change in any aeronautical facility, service, procedure, or hazard

questions.explanation: A NOTAM (Notice to Airmen) is a notice containing information essential to personnel concerned with flight operations. It covers: aerodrome closures, runway works, new obstacles, airspace restrictions, navigation aid outages, and other temporary or permanent changes. Pilots must check NOTAMs during pre-flight planning.

questions.question: The AIP (Aeronautical Information Publication) contains:-

options.text: permanent aeronautical information essential for air navigation

questions.explanation: The AIP is the primary publication containing permanent aeronautical information for a country. It includes: general information (regulations, services), en-route information (airspace, routes, navigation aids), and aerodrome information (charts, procedures, facilities). It is kept current through amendments, supplements, and AICs.

questions.question: The minimum flight time required for the issue of a private pilot licence (aeroplane) is:-

options.text: 45 hours, of which at least 25 hours must be dual and at least 15 hours must be solo

questions.explanation: The minimum flight time for a PPL(A) is 45 hours, comprising at least 25 hours dual instruction and at least 15 hours solo flight time. The solo time must include at least 5 hours of solo cross-country flight time, including one cross-country of at least 150 NM with full-stop landings at two different aerodromes.

questions.question: The solo cross-country requirement for a PPL includes a flight of at least:-

options.text: 150 NM with full-stop landings at two different aerodromes

questions.explanation: The PPL solo cross-country requirement includes at least one flight of 150 NM or more, with full-stop landings at two aerodromes different from the departure aerodrome. This demonstrates the student's ability to navigate, plan, and operate independently over a significant distance.

questions.question: A private pilot may not fly for hire or reward, except:-

options.text: the pilot may share the direct operating costs equally with passengers
the pilot may charge any amount
the pilot may never receive any payment
the pilot may charge for fuel only

questions.explanation: A private pilot may not fly for hire or reward. However, the pilot may share the direct operating costs (fuel, oil, landing fees, etc.) equally with the passengers. The pilot must pay their equal share. This is cost-sharing, not commercial operations. The pilot may not advertise or solicit passengers.

questions.question: The period of validity of a Class 2 medical for a private pilot aged 40 or over is:-
questions.explanation: Per SACAA CAR Part 67, for private pilots aged 40 and over, the Class 2 medical certificate is valid for 24 months (2 years), compared to 60 months for pilots under 40. The shorter validity period reflects the increased likelihood of medical conditions developing with age.

questions.question: An Aerodrome Traffic Zone (ATZ) extends from the surface to:-

options.text: a height published in the AIP above the aerodrome elevation

questions.explanation: An ATZ extends from the surface to a height published in the AIP (typically 2000-3000 ft above aerodrome elevation). It has a specified radius (usually 5 NM) centred on the aerodrome reference point. Within an ATZ, pilots must comply with the traffic pattern and maintain a listening watch on the appropriate frequency.

questions.question: The standard circuit height at an aerodrome is typically:-

options.text: 1000 ft above aerodrome elevation, unless otherwise published

questions.explanation: The standard circuit height is 1000 ft above aerodrome elevation (AAL), unless a different height is published in the AIP or indicated by local procedures. Some aerodromes may have different circuit heights for different aircraft types (e.g., lower for helicopters, higher for jets).

questions.question: When joining the circuit at an uncontrolled aerodrome, the standard procedure is to:-

options.text: overfly the aerodrome at circuit height or above, determine the runway in use, and join on the dead side descending to circuit height
fly straight in on final approach
join on the live side at any height

questions.explanation: At an uncontrolled aerodrome, the standard joining procedure is: overfly at circuit height or above to assess the wind direction, runway in use, and traffic. Then join on the dead side (opposite the circuit direction), descend to circuit height, and cross over to join the circuit. This provides the best situational awareness.

questions.question: The windsock at an aerodrome indicates:-

options.text: the surface wind direction and approximate speed

questions.explanation: The windsock shows both wind direction and approximate speed. It points in the direction the wind is blowing towards (downwind). A fully extended windsock indicates approximately 15 kt or more. A limp windsock indicates calm or very light winds. Aircraft take off and land into the wind.

questions.question: If deferral of the issuing of a South African medical certificate for a private pilot has to be made due to duty outside the Republic, such deferral shall not exceed:-

options.text: two consecutive periods each of three months
a single period of six months

questions.explanation: If a pilot is stationed outside South Africa and cannot renew their medical certificate, a deferral of up to two consecutive periods of three months each may be granted, subject to an acceptable medical report being obtained locally. This allows pilots working abroad to continue flying while arranging their SA medical.

questions.question: The air traffic services provided in controlled airspace include:-

options.text: air traffic control service, flight information service, and alerting service

questions.explanation: In controlled airspace, three services are provided: (1) Air Traffic Control (ATC) — separation of aircraft, (2) Flight Information Service (FIS) — weather, NOTAMs, traffic information, (3) Alerting Service — notification of search and rescue when an aircraft is in difficulty. In uncontrolled airspace, only FIS and alerting are provided.

questions.question: A Flight Information Service (FIS) provides:-

options.text: information useful for the safe and efficient conduct of flights

questions.explanation: FIS provides information useful for the safe and efficient conduct of flights, including: weather information, NOTAMs, aerodrome conditions, traffic information (where possible), and other relevant operational information. FIS does NOT provide separation — that is an ATC function in controlled airspace.

questions.question: The alerting service is activated when:-

options.text: an aircraft is believed to be in a state of uncertainty, alert, or distress
only when a pilot requests it

questions.explanation: The alerting service has three phases: INCERFA (uncertainty) — when an aircraft is overdue or communication is lost, ALERFA (alert) — when there is apprehension for the safety of the aircraft, DETRESFA (distress) — when there is reasonable certainty the aircraft is in danger. Each phase triggers escalating search and rescue responses.

questions.question: The minimum fuel reserve for a VFR flight by day is:-

options.text: fuel to fly to the destination plus 45 minutes reserve at normal cruise consumption
fuel to fly to the destination plus 30 minutes reserve
fuel to fly to the destination plus 60 minutes reserve
fuel to fly to the destination only

questions.explanation: For VFR day flights, the aircraft must carry sufficient fuel to fly to the destination plus a reserve of 45 minutes at normal cruise consumption. For VFR night flights, the reserve is also 45 minutes. This reserve accounts for headwinds, diversions, holding, and other contingencies.

questions.question: Before commencing a flight, the pilot-in-command must ensure that passengers are briefed on:-

options.text: the use of seat belts, emergency exits, and the location and use of emergency equipment

questions.explanation: The PIC must brief passengers on: use of seat belts (when to fasten and unfasten), location and operation of emergency exits, location and use of life jackets (if applicable), location of fire extinguisher, no smoking rules, and any other relevant safety information. This is required before every flight.

questions.question: Seat belts must be worn by all occupants during:-

options.text: take-off, landing, and whenever the pilot-in-command directs

questions.explanation: All occupants must wear seat belts during take-off, landing, and whenever the PIC directs (e.g., during turbulence, in the circuit). The PIC may also require seat belts to be worn throughout the flight. Shoulder harnesses, where fitted, must also be worn during take-off and landing.

questions.question: The wake turbulence category of a light aircraft is one with a maximum take-off mass of:-
questions.explanation: ICAO wake turbulence categories: Light (L) = 7000 kg or less MTOM, Medium (M) = more than 7000 kg but less than 136000 kg, Heavy (H) = 136000 kg or more, Super (J) = A380. Wake turbulence separation minima are based on these categories — a light aircraft following a heavy requires the greatest separation.

questions.question: The SACAA (South African Civil Aviation Authority) is responsible for:-

options.text: regulating and overseeing civil aviation safety in South Africa

questions.explanation: The SACAA is the regulatory authority responsible for civil aviation safety in South Africa. Its functions include: issuing licences and certificates, setting safety standards, conducting inspections and audits, investigating accidents and incidents, and enforcing compliance with aviation regulations.

questions.question: The Civil Aviation Act and Regulations in South Africa are based on the standards and recommended practices of:-
questions.explanation: South African aviation regulations are based on ICAO Standards and Recommended Practices (SARPs) as contained in the ICAO Annexes. South Africa, as a signatory to the Chicago Convention, is obligated to comply with ICAO standards or file differences where national regulations differ.

questions.question: The Chicago Convention of 1944 established:-

options.text: ICAO and the framework for international civil aviation

questions.explanation: The Convention on International Civil Aviation (Chicago Convention, 1944) established ICAO and set out the fundamental principles governing international air transport. It established sovereignty of airspace, aircraft nationality and registration, and the framework for international aviation standards through the ICAO Annexes.

questions.question: Each contracting state has complete and exclusive sovereignty over the airspace above its territory. This principle is established by:-
questions.explanation: Article 1 of the Chicago Convention states that every state has complete and exclusive sovereignty over the airspace above its territory. This means each country controls who may fly in its airspace and under what conditions. Foreign aircraft require permission to overfly or land in another state's territory.

questions.question: An aircraft registered in South Africa must display its nationality and registration marks. The nationality mark for South Africa is:-
questions.explanation: South African aircraft use nationality marks ZS (standard category), ZT (restricted category), or ZU (non-type-certificated/experimental). These are followed by a three-letter registration (e.g., ZS-ABC). The marks must be displayed on the aircraft as prescribed in the regulations.

questions.question: The standard VFR transponder code when not assigned a specific code by ATC is:-
questions.explanation: The standard conspicuity code for VFR flights (when no specific code has been assigned by ATC) is 1200 in South Africa. This allows ATC to identify VFR traffic on radar. In some countries, 7000 is used as the VFR conspicuity code.

questions.question: A flight plan may be closed by:-

options.text: the pilot reporting arrival to an ATS unit

questions.explanation: The pilot is responsible for closing the flight plan by reporting arrival to an ATS unit (by radio, telephone, or in person). If the flight plan is not closed, the alerting service may be activated, potentially triggering an unnecessary search and rescue operation. The flight plan should be closed as soon as possible after landing.

questions.question: If a pilot fails to close a flight plan after landing, the consequence may be:-

options.text: activation of the alerting service and possible search and rescue operations

questions.explanation: If a flight plan is not closed within a reasonable time after the estimated arrival time, the alerting service is activated. This progresses through INCERFA (uncertainty), ALERFA (alert), and DETRESFA (distress) phases, potentially triggering costly search and rescue operations. Pilots must always close their flight plans promptly.

questions.question: The minimum number of theoretical knowledge examinations that must be passed for a PPL(A) is:-
questions.explanation: The PPL(A) requires passing 9 theoretical knowledge examinations: Air Law, Aircraft Technical and General, Flight Performance and Planning, Human Performance, Meteorology, Navigation, Principles of Flight, Radio Communications, and Flight Planning. The pass mark is 75% for each subject.

questions.question: The pass mark for each PPL theoretical knowledge examination is:-
questions.explanation: The pass mark for each PPL theoretical knowledge examination is 75%. This is the standard across all SACAA PPL subjects. A candidate who fails a subject may re-sit the examination after a prescribed waiting period.

questions.question: A student pilot may not carry:-
questions.explanation: A student pilot flying solo may not carry passengers. The student pilot certificate only authorises solo flight (alone in the aircraft) or dual flight (with an instructor). Carrying passengers requires at least a private pilot licence.

questions.question: The validity period of a PPL theoretical knowledge examination pass is:-

options.text: 24 months from the date of the last subject passed

questions.explanation: PPL theoretical knowledge examination passes are valid for 24 months from the date the last subject was passed. All subjects must be passed and the skill test completed within this period. If the validity expires, the candidate may need to re-sit some or all examinations.

questions.question: An aircraft flying in the vicinity of an aerodrome shall:-

options.text: conform with or avoid the pattern of traffic formed by other aircraft in operation
fly at any altitude and in any direction

questions.explanation: An aircraft operating in the vicinity of an aerodrome must observe other traffic, conform with or avoid the traffic pattern, and make all turns to the left (unless right-hand circuits are indicated). This ensures orderly traffic flow and reduces the risk of collision in the busy aerodrome environment.

questions.question: An aircraft on the manoeuvring area of an aerodrome shall give way to:-

options.text: aircraft taking off or about to take off, and aircraft on final approach to land
no one — it always has priority

questions.explanation: An aircraft on the manoeuvring area must give way to aircraft taking off or about to take off, and to aircraft on final approach to land. An aircraft must not taxi onto a runway without ensuring there is no conflicting traffic on approach or departure. ATC clearance is required at controlled aerodromes.

questions.question: The term 'MAYDAY' is used to indicate:-

options.text: a distress condition — the aircraft is threatened by serious and/or imminent danger and requires immediate assistance

questions.explanation: MAYDAY (spoken three times) indicates a distress condition — the aircraft or persons on board are in serious and imminent danger and require immediate assistance. PAN PAN (spoken three times) indicates an urgency condition — a condition concerning the safety of the aircraft or persons but not requiring immediate assistance.

questions.question: The term 'PAN PAN' is used to indicate:-

options.text: an urgency condition — a condition concerning the safety of the aircraft but not requiring immediate assistance

questions.explanation: PAN PAN (spoken three times) indicates an urgency condition. This is less severe than MAYDAY — the aircraft is not in immediate danger but the situation could deteriorate. Examples: partial engine failure, low fuel, passenger medical emergency, uncertain of position. The pilot receives priority handling from ATC.

questions.question: The international emergency frequency is:-
questions.explanation: 121.5 MHz is the international aeronautical emergency frequency. It is monitored by ATC, military, and many commercial aircraft. Pilots should use this frequency when unable to establish communication on any other frequency, in an emergency, or when intercepted. ELTs (Emergency Locator Transmitters) also transmit on 121.5 MHz.

questions.question: Aerobatic flight is prohibited:-

options.text: over built-up areas, open-air assemblies, and within controlled airspace without ATC permission

questions.explanation: Aerobatic flight is prohibited: over built-up areas, over open-air assemblies of persons, within controlled airspace (without ATC permission), below a safe height for recovery, when flight visibility is less than 5 km, and when passengers are carried unless they have given consent and the aircraft is certificated for aerobatics.

questions.question: No person shall drop any object from an aircraft in flight except:-

options.text: with the permission of the Commissioner or in an emergency
at any time over open water

questions.explanation: Dropping objects from an aircraft is prohibited except with the Commissioner's permission or in an emergency. This includes jettisoning fuel, dropping supplies, or any other object. Exceptions exist for agricultural operations, firefighting, and other approved activities conducted under specific permits.

questions.question: An aircraft may not tow another aircraft or object except:-

options.text: in accordance with conditions prescribed by the Commissioner

questions.explanation: Towing (of gliders, banners, or other objects) is only permitted in accordance with conditions prescribed by the Commissioner. The towing aircraft must be properly equipped and the pilot must be qualified. Specific procedures and limitations apply to each type of towing operation.

questions.question: Formation flight is only permitted when:-

options.text: pre-arranged between the pilots-in-command of all aircraft involved
all aircraft are the same type

questions.explanation: Formation flight must be pre-arranged between the PICs of all aircraft. The formation must not be flown through cloud or in conditions of reduced visibility. In controlled airspace, ATC must be informed. Only one aircraft files a flight plan on behalf of the formation. Formation flight over built-up areas is prohibited.

questions.question: The responsibility for maintaining an aircraft in an airworthy condition rests with:-

options.text: the owner or operator of the aircraft

questions.explanation: The owner or operator is responsible for maintaining the aircraft in an airworthy condition. This includes: complying with the approved maintenance programme, ensuring all airworthiness directives are complied with, keeping maintenance records, and ensuring the aircraft is not flown with known defects that affect airworthiness.

questions.question: An ELT (Emergency Locator Transmitter) transmits on:-
questions.explanation: Modern ELTs transmit on both 121.5 MHz (the international aeronautical emergency frequency) and 406 MHz (the satellite-monitored frequency). The 406 MHz signal is detected by the COSPAS-SARSAT satellite system, providing accurate position information to search and rescue services.

questions.question: The white flashes from the control tower to an aircraft on the ground means:-

options.text: return to starting point on the aerodrome

questions.explanation: White flashes directed at an aircraft on the ground mean return to your starting point (parking position) on the aerodrome. This is used when the aircraft needs to return to the apron, perhaps due to a change in conditions or a problem that needs to be resolved before flight.

questions.question: A flight plan for a VFR flight must include:-

options.text: aircraft identification, flight rules, departure aerodrome, route, destination, estimated times, and fuel endurance

questions.explanation: A flight plan must include: aircraft identification (registration), flight rules (VFR/IFR), type of aircraft, departure aerodrome and time, route, cruising level and speed, destination aerodrome, estimated elapsed time, fuel endurance, number of persons on board, emergency equipment, and pilot's name.

questions.question: An air traffic service flight plan must be filed for a flight from a manned aerodrome to an aerodrome traffic zone where no other controlled or advisory airspace will be entered during the flight:-

options.text: true — a flight plan is required between ATZs
false — no flight plan is needed
only if the flight is at night
only if the flight exceeds 100 NM

questions.explanation: A flight plan is required for flights between aerodrome traffic zones, even if no controlled or advisory airspace is entered en route. This ensures ATC/FIS at both aerodromes is aware of the flight and can activate the alerting service if the aircraft fails to arrive.

questions.question: The pilot-in-command shall ensure that the aircraft's position lights (navigation lights) are displayed:-

options.text: from sunset to sunrise, or at any other time when visibility is reduced
at all times, day and night

questions.explanation: Navigation lights (red on the left wing, green on the right wing, white on the tail) must be displayed from sunset to sunrise and at any other time when the PIC considers it necessary due to reduced visibility. They help other pilots determine the direction of travel of the aircraft.

questions.question: The red navigation light is on the:-
questions.explanation: Navigation light colours: Red on the left (port) wing, Green on the right (starboard) wing, White on the tail. A useful memory aid: 'port wine is red' (port = left = red). If you see a red light on your right and a green on your left, the other aircraft is coming towards you.

questions.question: The green navigation light is on the:-
questions.explanation: The green navigation light is on the right (starboard) wing. Combined with the red light on the left wing and white light on the tail, these lights allow other pilots to determine the aircraft's direction of travel at night. Each light is visible through a specific arc.

questions.question: If you observe another aircraft at night showing a red light on your left and a green light on your right, the aircraft is:-
questions.explanation: If you see red on your left and green on your right, the other aircraft's port (red) side is on your left and starboard (green) side is on your right — it is heading towards you. Both aircraft should alter heading to the right. If you see only a red light, the aircraft is crossing from right to left and has right of way.

questions.question: The term 'flight time' for a pilot means:-

options.text: the total time from the moment the aircraft first moves under its own power for the purpose of taking off until it comes to rest at the end of the flight
only the time in the air
the time from engine start to engine shutdown
the time from leaving the gate to arriving at the gate

questions.explanation: Flight time (also called block time) is measured from when the aircraft first moves under its own power for the purpose of taking off until it comes to rest at the end of the flight. This includes taxi time. For logbook purposes, this is the time that counts towards experience requirements and flight time limitations.

questions.question: A defect discovered during a pre-flight inspection that affects the airworthiness of the aircraft must be:-

options.text: recorded in the aircraft flight folio and rectified before flight
ignored if the flight is short
only reported if it causes an accident

questions.explanation: Any defect affecting airworthiness must be recorded in the aircraft flight folio (technical log) and rectified by an appropriately licensed engineer before the aircraft may fly. The PIC must not fly an aircraft with a known unserviceability that affects airworthiness. Some minor defects may be deferred under an approved MEL (Minimum Equipment List).

questions.question: The holder of a PPL may act as pilot-in-command of:-

options.text: an aircraft of the type and class for which the licence is valid, but not for hire or reward

questions.explanation: A PPL holder may act as PIC of an aircraft of the type and class endorsed on the licence, but not for hire or reward (except cost-sharing). The PPL does not authorise commercial operations. The pilot must also hold a valid medical certificate and meet recency requirements.

questions.question: The revalidation period for a PPL is:-
questions.explanation: A PPL must be revalidated every 24 months (2 years). Revalidation requires passing a skill test with a designated flight examiner. The pilot must have flown at least 3 hours as PIC in the preceding 6 months before the test. If the licence lapses, renewal (more extensive) procedures apply.

questions.question: The difference between revalidation and renewal of a pilot licence is:-

options.text: revalidation is done before expiry; renewal is done after the licence has expired
renewal is only for commercial pilots

questions.explanation: Revalidation is the process of extending the validity of a current (not yet expired) licence by passing a skill test. Renewal is the process of restoring the validity of an expired licence, which typically requires additional training, a more comprehensive skill test, and possibly re-examination of theoretical knowledge.

questions.question: Smoking on board an aircraft is:-
questions.explanation: Smoking is prohibited on board all aircraft at all times. This includes electronic cigarettes. Smoking is a fire hazard in the confined, oxygen-enriched environment of an aircraft. The PIC must ensure compliance and brief passengers accordingly before each flight.

questions.question: The minimum equipment required for VFR day flight includes:-

options.text: ASI, altimeter, magnetic compass, tachometer (or manifold pressure gauge), oil pressure and temperature gauges, fuel quantity indicator, and a timepiece

questions.explanation: Minimum instruments for VFR day: airspeed indicator, altimeter (sensitive), magnetic compass, tachometer (or MP gauge for CSU engines), oil pressure gauge, oil temperature gauge, fuel quantity indicator for each tank, and a timepiece showing hours, minutes, and seconds. Additional instruments are required for night and IFR flight.

questions.question: For VFR flight at night, in addition to day VFR instruments, the aircraft must also be equipped with:-

options.text: attitude indicator, heading indicator, turn and slip indicator, and a sensitive altimeter

questions.explanation: Night VFR requires additional instruments beyond day VFR: attitude indicator (artificial horizon), heading indicator (DI), turn and slip indicator (or turn coordinator), and a sensitive altimeter. These are essentially the basic IFR instruments, because visual references are limited at night.

questions.question: The pilot-in-command must carry their pilot licence and medical certificate:-

options.text: on their person or readily accessible in the aircraft during flight

questions.explanation: The pilot must have their licence and medical certificate on their person or readily accessible in the aircraft during every flight. These documents must be produced on demand to an authorised person (inspector, police officer). Flying without valid documents is an offence.

questions.question: An Airworthiness Directive (AD) is:-

options.text: a mandatory instruction issued by the aviation authority requiring specific maintenance or modification to an aircraft

questions.explanation: An Airworthiness Directive (AD) is a legally enforceable rule issued by the aviation authority when an unsafe condition is found in an aircraft, engine, propeller, or appliance. Compliance is mandatory within the specified timeframe. Failure to comply renders the aircraft unairworthy.

questions.question: The 'date of application' when used in connection with the issuing of a licence means:-

options.text: the date on which the application is received in the prescribed form by the Commissioner
the date the pilot passes the skill test
the date the pilot starts training
the date the licence is collected

questions.explanation: The 'date of application' is the date on which the completed application form is received by the Commissioner (SACAA). This date is important for determining validity periods and processing timelines. The application must be in the prescribed form and accompanied by all required documents.

questions.question: An applicant for a night rating must have completed 10 hours of instrument instruction of which not more than:-

options.text: 5 hours may have been acquired in an approved FSTD
3 hours may have been in an FSTD
8 hours may have been in an FSTD
all 10 hours may be in an FSTD

questions.explanation: Of the 10 hours of instrument instruction required for a night rating, a maximum of 5 hours may be completed in an approved Flight Simulation Training Device (FSTD). The remaining 5 hours must be actual instrument flight time in an aircraft. This ensures adequate real-world instrument flying experience.

questions.question: The FIR (Flight Information Region) in South Africa is managed by:-
questions.explanation: ATNS (Air Traffic and Navigation Services) is the air navigation service provider in South Africa. It manages the FIR, provides air traffic control, flight information, and alerting services. SACAA is the regulator (sets rules), while ATNS is the service provider (operates ATC). ACSA (Airports Company South Africa) manages major airports.

questions.question: Advisory airspace is airspace where:-

options.text: an air traffic advisory service is available but ATC separation is not provided

questions.explanation: Advisory airspace (advisory routes/areas) provides an air traffic advisory service — traffic information and conflict advice — but does not provide ATC separation. Pilots are advised of known traffic but remain responsible for their own separation. A flight plan is required to enter advisory airspace.

questions.question: The South African FIR is divided into:-

options.text: upper and lower airspace, with the boundary typically at FL245

questions.explanation: The South African FIR is divided into lower airspace (below FL245) and upper airspace (FL245 and above). The upper airspace is designated as Upper Flight Information Region (UIR). Different rules and services may apply in each. Most PPL operations take place in the lower airspace.

questions.question: ICAO Annex 2 deals with:-
questions.explanation: ICAO Annex 2 covers Rules of the Air — the international standards for flight rules, right of way, signals, and general operating procedures. Key ICAO Annexes: Annex 1 = Personnel Licensing, Annex 2 = Rules of the Air, Annex 3 = Meteorological Service, Annex 8 = Airworthiness, Annex 11 = Air Traffic Services.

questions.question: ICAO Annex 1 deals with:-
questions.explanation: ICAO Annex 1 covers Personnel Licensing — the international standards for pilot licences, ratings, medical certificates, and flight crew qualifications. South African licensing requirements are based on these ICAO standards.

questions.question: A pilot who witnesses an accident must:-

options.text: render all possible assistance and report the accident to the Commissioner or an ATSU as soon as possible
continue the flight and report later
report to the local police only

questions.explanation: Any person who witnesses an aircraft accident must render all possible assistance to survivors and report the accident to the Commissioner or an ATSU as soon as possible. The witness should note the location, time, and circumstances. Failure to render assistance or report may be an offence.

questions.question: The difference between an accident and an incident is:-

options.text: an accident involves death, serious injury, or substantial aircraft damage; an incident is any other occurrence affecting safety
an incident is more serious than an accident

questions.explanation: An accident involves: death or serious injury, or substantial damage to the aircraft, occurring between the time any person boards with the intention of flight until all persons have disembarked. An incident is any occurrence (other than an accident) that affects or could affect the safety of operations. Both must be reported.

questions.question: Noise abatement procedures at an aerodrome are established to:-

options.text: minimise the impact of aircraft noise on communities near the aerodrome

questions.explanation: Noise abatement procedures are designed to reduce the noise impact on residential areas near aerodromes. They may include: preferred runways, specific departure and arrival routes, altitude restrictions, power reduction procedures, and curfew hours. Pilots must comply with published noise abatement procedures.

questions.question: A pilot who becomes aware of a bird hazard at or near an aerodrome should:-

options.text: report it to ATC or the aerodrome authority
only report if a bird strike occurs

questions.explanation: Bird hazards should be reported to ATC or the aerodrome authority immediately. Bird strikes can cause significant damage to aircraft, including engine failure. ATC can warn other aircraft and the aerodrome authority can take action to disperse the birds. A bird strike must also be reported.

questions.question: The holding position marking on a taxiway (two solid and two dashed yellow lines) indicates:-

options.text: the point beyond which an aircraft must not proceed without ATC clearance

questions.explanation: The holding position marking (two solid yellow lines and two dashed yellow lines across the taxiway) indicates the boundary of the runway strip. An aircraft must not cross this marking without ATC clearance at a controlled aerodrome. The solid lines are on the taxiway side; the dashed lines are on the runway side.

questions.question: Runway numbers are based on:-

options.text: the magnetic bearing of the runway rounded to the nearest 10 degrees
the true bearing of the runway
the order in which runways were built

questions.explanation: Runway numbers are the magnetic bearing of the runway direction divided by 10 and rounded to the nearest whole number. For example, a runway with a magnetic bearing of 074° would be designated Runway 07. The reciprocal runway would be 25 (074 + 180 = 254°). Parallel runways add L, C, or R suffixes.

questions.question: The white threshold markings at the beginning of a runway indicate:-

options.text: the beginning of the runway available for landing
