questions.explanation: White threshold markings (stripes across the runway width) indicate the beginning of the runway surface available for landing. The number of stripes indicates the runway width. A displaced threshold (marked with arrows) means the portion before the threshold is available for take-off and taxi but not for landing.

questions.question: A displaced threshold means:-

options.text: the landing threshold has been moved from the beginning of the runway; the area before it may be used for take-off but not for landing
the runway is shortened for all operations
only helicopters may use the runway

questions.explanation: A displaced threshold is indicated by white arrows pointing towards the threshold marking. The area before the displaced threshold may be used for take-off, taxi, and landing rollout, but not for landing (touchdown). The threshold is displaced due to obstacles on the approach path or other safety reasons.

questions.question: Yellow chevrons (arrowheads) painted on a runway surface indicate:-

options.text: a stopway or blast pad — not available for any aircraft operations

questions.explanation: Yellow chevrons indicate a stopway, blast pad, or overrun area that is not suitable for aircraft operations (taxiing, take-off, or landing). This area may not support the weight of aircraft and is only intended as a safety buffer beyond the runway end.

questions.question: The pilot-in-command of an aircraft involved in a near-miss (airprox) should:-

options.text: file an airprox report with the appropriate authority
only report if contact was made

questions.explanation: An airprox (air proximity) report should be filed whenever a pilot believes the safety of the aircraft was compromised by the proximity of another aircraft. The report is filed with the appropriate authority (ATSU or SACAA) and is used to investigate and prevent future occurrences. It is not punitive — it is a safety tool.

questions.question: The minimum rest period for a flight crew member before commencing flight duty is:-

options.text: as prescribed in the regulations, typically at least 10 consecutive hours including an opportunity for 8 hours sleep

questions.explanation: Flight crew members must have adequate rest before commencing duty. The regulations prescribe minimum rest periods (typically at least 10 consecutive hours including an opportunity for 8 hours of uninterrupted sleep). Fatigue is a significant safety hazard — a fatigued pilot must not fly.

questions.question: A pilot must not fly an aircraft unless they are satisfied that:-

options.text: the aircraft is fit to fly, the flight can be made safely, and all regulatory requirements are met

questions.explanation: Before every flight, the PIC must be satisfied that: the aircraft is airworthy and properly equipped, the aircraft is loaded within limits, sufficient fuel is on board, weather conditions are suitable, the flight can be completed safely, and all regulatory requirements are met. This is the PIC's overarching responsibility.

questions.question: The term 'aerodrome elevation' means:-

options.text: the elevation of the highest point of the landing area
the elevation of the control tower
the elevation of the lowest point of the runway
the average elevation of the surrounding terrain

questions.explanation: Aerodrome elevation is the elevation of the highest point of the landing area, measured above mean sea level. This is used for altimeter setting, circuit height calculation, and performance planning. It is published in the AIP for each aerodrome.

questions.question: The term 'aerodrome reference point' (ARP) is:-

options.text: the designated geographical location of an aerodrome, usually near the centre of the landing area
the threshold of the main runway

questions.explanation: The Aerodrome Reference Point (ARP) is the designated geographical location (latitude and longitude) of an aerodrome, typically near the geometric centre of the landing area. It is used as the reference for measuring distances, defining ATZ boundaries, and for navigation purposes.

questions.question: A pilot flying VFR who encounters deteriorating weather should:-

options.text: turn back or divert to an aerodrome with better conditions before entering IMC
descend to low level and continue

questions.explanation: A VFR pilot encountering deteriorating weather must turn back or divert before entering IMC. Continuing into IMC is one of the most common causes of fatal GA accidents. The pilot should: maintain visual reference, turn back to better conditions, divert to a suitable aerodrome, and if necessary declare an emergency.

questions.question: The semi-circular rule for VFR flights uses:-

options.text: magnetic track to determine the appropriate cruising level

questions.explanation: The semi-circular (cruising level) rule uses the magnetic track of the aircraft to determine the appropriate flight level. Tracks 000°-179° magnetic use odd thousands plus 500 ft (FL045, FL065, FL075...). Tracks 180°-359° magnetic use even thousands plus 500 ft (FL055, FL075...). This provides vertical separation between opposing traffic.

questions.question: For VFR flights, the semi-circular cruising levels for a magnetic track of 090° would include:-
questions.explanation: Magnetic track 090° is in the range 000-179°, so VFR cruising levels are odd thousands plus 500 ft: FL045 (4500 ft), FL065 (6500 ft), FL085 (8500 ft), FL105 (10500 ft), etc. IFR flights on the same track range use odd thousands: FL050, FL070, FL090, etc.

questions.question: For VFR flights, the semi-circular cruising levels for a magnetic track of 270° would include:-
questions.explanation: Magnetic track 270° is in the range 180-359°, so VFR cruising levels are even thousands plus 500 ft: FL055 (5500 ft), FL075 (7500 ft), FL095 (9500 ft), FL115 (11500 ft), etc. IFR flights on the same track range use even thousands: FL060, FL080, FL100, etc.

questions.question: An aircraft on a VFR flight entering controlled airspace must:-

options.text: file a flight plan after landing

questions.explanation: A VFR flight must obtain ATC clearance before entering controlled airspace. The pilot must contact ATC, state their intentions, and receive a clearance (which may include specific routing, altitude, and transponder code). Entering controlled airspace without clearance is a serious violation.

questions.question: A readback of an ATC clearance is required for:-

options.text: all route clearances, level instructions, heading instructions, speed instructions, and runway assignments

questions.explanation: Pilots must read back: route clearances, level (altitude/flight level) instructions, heading instructions, speed instructions, SSR codes, altimeter settings, runway in use, and any clearance to enter, land on, take off from, hold short of, cross, or backtrack on any runway. This ensures the pilot has correctly received the instruction.

questions.question: The phrase 'WILCO' in radio communications means:-

options.text: I understand your message and will comply

questions.explanation: WILCO means 'I have received your message, understand it, and will comply with it.' It should not be used for instructions that require a readback. ROGER means 'I have received your message' (acknowledgement only, not compliance). AFFIRM means 'yes.' NEGATIVE means 'no.'

questions.question: The phrase 'ROGER' in radio communications means:-

options.text: I have received all of your last transmission
I will comply with your instruction

questions.explanation: ROGER means 'I have received all of your last transmission.' It is an acknowledgement only — it does NOT mean the pilot will comply. WILCO means 'I will comply.' ROGER and WILCO should never be used together. ROGER should not be used for instructions requiring a readback.

questions.question: QNH is the altimeter setting that causes the altimeter to read:-
questions.explanation: QNH is the atmospheric pressure at mean sea level. When set on the altimeter subscale, the altimeter reads altitude above mean sea level (AMSL). QNH is used for flights below the transition altitude. On the ground at an aerodrome, the altimeter should read the aerodrome elevation when QNH is set.

questions.question: QFE is the altimeter setting that causes the altimeter to read:-

options.text: height above the aerodrome elevation (zero on the ground)

questions.explanation: QFE is the atmospheric pressure at the aerodrome elevation. When set on the altimeter subscale, the altimeter reads height above the aerodrome (zero on the ground at that aerodrome). QFE is useful in the circuit for maintaining accurate circuit height. It is less commonly used than QNH in South Africa.

questions.question: The transition altitude in South Africa is:-

options.text: the altitude at or below which vertical position is expressed as altitude (QNH), published for each area
the same as the transition level

questions.explanation: The transition altitude is the altitude at or below which the vertical position of an aircraft is expressed as altitude (using QNH). Above the transition level, vertical position is expressed as flight levels (using standard pressure 1013.25 hPa). The transition altitude varies by area and is published in the AIP.

questions.question: When flying at a flight level, the altimeter is set to:-
questions.explanation: When flying at a flight level (above the transition altitude), the altimeter is set to the standard pressure setting of 1013.25 hPa (29.92 inHg). This ensures all aircraft at flight levels are using the same reference, providing consistent vertical separation regardless of local pressure variations.

questions.question: For VFR flight at night in uncontrolled airspace, the minimum visibility required is:-
questions.explanation: For VFR night flight in uncontrolled airspace, the minimum visibility is 5 km. The pilot must also maintain the prescribed distance from cloud (1500 m horizontally, 1000 ft vertically above 3000 ft AMSL). Night VFR requires a night rating and additional equipment.

questions.question: Class C airspace in South Africa is:-

options.text: controlled airspace where both IFR and VFR flights are permitted, and ATC provides separation between all flights

questions.explanation: Class C is controlled airspace where IFR and VFR flights are permitted. ATC provides separation between IFR/IFR, IFR/VFR, and VFR/VFR flights. ATC clearance is required. Speed limit of 250 kt below FL100 applies. Two-way radio communication and transponder are required.

questions.question: Class D airspace in South Africa is:-

options.text: controlled airspace where IFR and VFR flights are permitted; ATC provides separation between IFR flights and traffic information to VFR flights

questions.explanation: Class D is controlled airspace where IFR and VFR flights are permitted with ATC clearance. ATC provides separation between IFR flights and traffic information between IFR and VFR, and between VFR flights. VFR flights are responsible for their own separation from other VFR traffic based on the information provided.

questions.question: Third party liability insurance for an aircraft is:-

options.text: compulsory — the aircraft may not be flown without valid insurance

questions.explanation: Third party liability insurance is compulsory for all aircraft. The aircraft may not be flown without valid insurance covering liability for damage to third parties on the ground and in the air. The insurance certificate must be carried on board the aircraft.

questions.question: The pilot-in-command has the final authority regarding the operation of the aircraft. This means:-

options.text: the PIC may refuse to fly or may deviate from any instruction if safety requires it
the PIC must always follow ATC instructions
the PIC must always follow the operator's instructions
the PIC has no authority over passengers

questions.explanation: The PIC has final authority and responsibility for the operation of the aircraft. This means the PIC may refuse to fly if they consider the flight unsafe, may deviate from any rule or ATC instruction in an emergency, and has authority over all persons on board. This authority comes with corresponding responsibility.

questions.question: A pilot who has been prescribed medication must:-

options.text: not fly unless the medication has been approved by a designated aviation medical examiner
fly normally if they feel fine
only avoid flying for 24 hours after taking medication

questions.explanation: A pilot must not fly while taking any medication unless it has been specifically approved by a designated aviation medical examiner (DAME). Many common medications (antihistamines, sedatives, some antibiotics) have side effects that can impair flying ability. When in doubt, consult the DAME before flying.

questions.question: The minimum time between consuming alcohol and acting as a flight crew member is:-
questions.explanation: The '8 hours bottle to throttle' rule requires at least 8 hours between consuming alcohol and acting as a flight crew member. However, even after 8 hours, if the blood alcohol level exceeds 0.02% or the pilot is still impaired, they must not fly. The effects of alcohol can persist well beyond 8 hours.

questions.question: Scuba diving before flying is dangerous because:-

options.text: dissolved nitrogen in the blood can form bubbles at altitude, causing decompression sickness
it has no effect on flying

questions.explanation: After scuba diving, dissolved nitrogen remains in the blood and tissues. At altitude (reduced pressure), this nitrogen can form bubbles causing decompression sickness ('the bends'). The recommended waiting time is at least 12 hours after non-decompression diving and 24 hours after decompression diving before flying.

questions.question: The VFR weather minima below 1500 ft AGL in uncontrolled airspace by day require:-

options.text: clear of cloud, in sight of the surface, and flight visibility of at least 5 km
5 km visibility and 1000 ft vertical from cloud
8 km visibility and 2000 ft horizontal from cloud

questions.explanation: Below 1500 ft AGL in uncontrolled airspace by day, VFR weather minima are: clear of cloud, in sight of the surface, and flight visibility of at least 5 km. These are less restrictive than above 1500 ft AGL (where specific cloud clearance distances apply) because at low level, terrain avoidance is the primary concern.

questions.question: An AIC (Aeronautical Information Circular) contains:-

options.text: information of an explanatory or advisory nature that does not qualify for inclusion in the AIP or NOTAMs

questions.explanation: An AIC contains information that is explanatory or advisory in nature, such as: changes to regulations, new procedures, safety recommendations, and administrative information. AICs do not qualify for inclusion in the AIP (which contains permanent information) or NOTAMs (which contain time-critical information).

questions.question: An AIP Supplement (AIP SUP) is used to publish:-

options.text: temporary changes of long duration or permanent changes of short duration that contain extensive text and/or graphics

questions.explanation: AIP Supplements are used for temporary changes of long duration (3 months or more) or permanent changes involving extensive text/graphics that cannot be easily incorporated into the AIP by amendment. Examples include: temporary airspace restrictions for major events, extended runway closures, or new procedures being trialled.

questions.question: The pilot-in-command must ensure that all passengers are seated with seat belts fastened during:-

options.text: take-off, landing, and whenever the PIC considers it necessary for safety

questions.explanation: Passengers must be seated with seat belts fastened during take-off, landing, and whenever the PIC directs. The PIC has discretion to require seat belts at any time during the flight for safety reasons (e.g., turbulence, low-level flight). It is good practice to keep seat belts loosely fastened throughout the flight.

questions.question: A pilot who is involved in an enforcement action by the SACAA has the right to:-

options.text: appeal the decision through the prescribed legal process
continue flying pending appeal in all cases

questions.explanation: A pilot subject to enforcement action has the right to appeal through the prescribed legal process. The Civil Aviation Act provides for administrative review and appeal procedures. However, if a licence is suspended on safety grounds, the suspension typically takes effect immediately pending the outcome of the appeal.

questions.question: The green flashes from the control tower to an aircraft in flight means:-

options.text: return for landing (you are cleared to rejoin the circuit)

questions.explanation: Green flashes to an aircraft in flight mean 'return for landing' — the aircraft should rejoin the circuit and prepare to land. This is different from a steady green (cleared to land) and is used to recall aircraft that may have departed the circuit area or to indicate the aircraft should prepare for an approach.

questions.question: A white cross displayed on a runway or taxiway indicates:-

options.text: the runway or taxiway is closed and unfit for aircraft movement
the runway is available for landing

questions.explanation: A white cross displayed on a runway or taxiway indicates that it is closed and unfit for aircraft movement. Aircraft must not use a closed runway or taxiway. The cross may be displayed as a physical marker or painted on the surface.

questions.question: The signal area at an aerodrome is:-

options.text: a designated area where ground signals are displayed to provide information to pilots

questions.explanation: The signal area is a designated area on the aerodrome (usually near the control tower or in a prominent position) where ground signals are displayed. These include: landing direction indicator (T), wind direction indicator (windsock), circuit direction arrows, and special signals (X for landing prohibited, dumbbell, etc.).

questions.question: A double white cross displayed in the signal area indicates:-

options.text: glider flying is taking place at the aerodrome

questions.explanation: A double white cross in the signal area indicates that glider flying is taking place. Pilots should exercise extra caution as gliders may be operating in the circuit, on tow, or thermalling near the aerodrome. Gliders have right of way over powered aircraft.

questions.question: A red L-shaped marker displayed in the signal area indicates:-

options.text: the direction in which right-hand circuits are to be made

questions.explanation: A red L-shaped marker (or arrow) in the signal area indicates the direction of right-hand circuits for the associated runway. The arm of the L points in the direction of the right-hand turn. If no such marker is displayed, standard left-hand circuits apply.

questions.question: The pilot-in-command of an aircraft shall not commence a flight unless satisfied that the aircraft has sufficient fuel to:-

options.text: complete the planned flight safely with the required reserves

questions.explanation: The PIC must ensure sufficient fuel is on board to complete the planned flight safely with the required reserves (45 minutes for VFR day/night). The fuel calculation must account for: taxi, climb, cruise, descent, approach, and reserves. Headwinds, diversions, and contingencies must be considered.

questions.question: The IMSAFE checklist used by pilots before flight stands for:-

options.text: Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue, Eating/Emotion
Instruments, Maps, Speed, Altitude, Fuel, Engine
Ice, Meteorology, Safety, Airspace, Flight plan, Equipment
Inspection, Maintenance, Systems, Avionics, Fuel, Electrical

questions.explanation: IMSAFE is a personal fitness checklist: Illness (am I sick?), Medication (am I taking any?), Stress (am I under excessive stress?), Alcohol (have I consumed alcohol in the last 8 hours?), Fatigue (am I adequately rested?), Eating/Emotion (have I eaten properly? Am I emotionally fit?). A 'yes' to any may mean the pilot should not fly.
